founder.name: Derek Osei
founder.notes: 8 years running Osei Aerial, a single-operator FAA Part 107 drone-inspection business focused on post-hailstorm roof inspections for insurance claims across the TX/OK Hail Alley corridor. Pivoting from solo operator to a two-sided marketplace. Wants to raise a seed round.

business_basics.one_liner: A booking marketplace that lets roofing contractors doing storm-damage insurance claims summon a vetted, FAA Part 107-certified drone pilot within a 30-mile radius to fly and deliver an insurance-ready roof inspection report within 24 hours of a hailstorm, instead of scrambling their own crew or waiting days for a scheduling gap.
business_basics.business_type_notes: Two-sided marketplace: supply = independent FAA Part 107-certified drone pilots (freelancers and 2-5 person shops); demand = storm-damage insurance-claim roofing contractors (10-50 crews), TX/OK Hail Alley corridor. Transaction = per-property booking; demand pays a flat job price ($175/property), marketplace retains an 18% take rate, remits the rest to the pilot. Supply is the binding liquidity constraint (thin, unproven pool); demand is Derek's stronger existing network (former direct Osei Aerial clients). Demand is spiky/event-driven (triggered by specific hailstorms), not steady-state. A critical external veto-holder exists on the demand side: the insurance carrier/adjuster must accept SkyClaim's report format as valid claim documentation, or contractors won't adopt regardless of price or speed.

01_market_segmentation.summary: 13 candidate segments identified (6 supply-side, 7 demand-side), brainstormed separately per marketplace convention; shortlisted for Step 2: storm-damage roofing contractors + public adjusters (demand), freelance/small-shop pilots + retired ag-survey pilots (supply)

02_select_a_beachhead_market.summary: Beachhead selected: storm-damage roofing contractors (demand) paired with freelance/small-shop drone pilots (supply), TX/OK Hail Alley — the only pairing reachable on both sides simultaneously

03_build_an_end_user_profile.summary: Two full profiles drafted (supply: 8 real pilot conversations; demand: 6 real contractor conversations, all existing Osei Aerial clients) — both samples flagged as network-biased

04_calculate_the_tam_for_the_beachhead_m.summary: Beachhead TAM ≈$880K/year, supply-constrained (350 theoretical pilots x 80 properties/yr x $175 x 18% take rate); far below this step's own workable-beachhead heuristic — flagged as a possible methodology gap for marketplaces, not silently treated as disqualifying

05_profile_the_persona_for_the_beachhead.summary: Primary persona: Marcus Webb, independent pilot (supply, the harder-constraint side) — grounded in a real interview; secondary demand-side persona (Big Ray Delgado) also drafted

06_full_life_cycle_use_case.summary: Two separate 8-stage tracks mapped (supply: Marcus; demand: Ray); biggest drop-off risk: demand-side liquidity-visibility at the evaluation stage

07_high_level_product_specification.summary: 5 Must-have capabilities covering both sides (job board, upload, booking flow, report delivery, payment split); core flow traced to both FLCUC tracks

08_quantify_the_value_proposition.summary: Quantified separately per side: supply ≈$300-525/month incremental income (marginal-to-sufficient); demand value directional/unquantified (capacity-unlock, not forced into a number)

09_identify_your_next_10_customers.summary: 10 prospects listed (5 supply, 5 demand), 8 of 10 real/contacted; demand side is Derek's stronger network (inverse of the general marketplace pattern) — flagged explicitly

10_define_your_core.summary: No durable Core yet — honest finding per this step's own marketplace guidance (pre-liquidity marketplace); current advantage is a personal moat (Derek's domain expertise/relationships), not a Core

11_chart_your_competitive_position.summary: Two separate positioning maps (supply and demand face different alternatives); both target positions unoccupied but unearned — not yet defensible per Step 10's finding

12_determine_the_dmu.summary: Two full DMU tables per marketplace template — supply collapses to 1 person; demand has 2-3 roles plus a critical external veto-holder (the insurance carrier)

13_map_the_process_to_acquire_a_paying_c.summary: Two parallel 5-stage acquisition maps (supply, demand); riskiest stage: demand-side carrier-acceptance check, unresolved and external to SkyClaim's control

14_calculate_the_tam_for_follow_on_marke.summary: Pin 2 (public adjusters, same supply pool) ≈$150K/yr take-rate TAM, flagged as supply-contention risk not pure incremental revenue; Pin 3 (Colorado) not sized — no basis yet

15_design_a_business_model.summary: Selected model: marketplace take-rate, demand pays full price, supply charged nothing (protects the binding-constraint side); subscription/listing-fee/fee-for-service rejected as mismatched

16_set_your_pricing_framework.summary: Pricing: $175/property (demand pays, sourced from Derek's own 3-year operating history), 18% take rate (untested, anchored to category benchmark)

17_calculate_the_ltv_of_a_customer.summary: Demand-side-only LTV ≈$3,750/contractor (all inputs low confidence); this step has no marketplace guidance, forcing an undocumented scope choice — flagged as a cross-step gap with Step 19

18_map_the_sales_process_to_acquire_a_cu.summary: Two separate costed funnels (supply ≈$225/pilot, demand ≈$300/contractor floor); this step also has no marketplace guidance despite Step 13 producing two processes — improvised two tables

19_calculate_the_coca.summary: Demand-side LTV:COCA ≈12.5:1 (provisional, floor COCA); supply-side COCA ≈$225/pilot reported with NO corresponding LTV — reported as N/A rather than forced, demonstrating the Step 17/18 marketplace gap concretely

20_identify_key_assumptions.summary: 31-item register swept from Steps 1-19 (29 key_assumptions + 2 flagged quantitative_claims); top leap-of-faith item: carrier acceptance of the report format (ka-012)

21_test_key_assumptions.summary: All 8 shortlisted leap-of-faith assumptions deferred (pivot/pre-MVBP stage); full-inventory disposition recorded for every other entry; biggest open risk carried forward: carrier acceptance (ka-012)

22_define_the_mvbp.summary: MVBP: real $175/property bookings via manual concierge matching, supply sourced first (the harder liquidity side); success = 3 real transactions in 6 weeks with 1 carrier-accepted report

23_show_that_dogs_will_eat_the_dog_food.summary: Not yet measurable — no MVBP transaction has occurred; Osei Aerial's own 78% legacy-client rebooking rate noted as directional context only, not marketplace evidence

24_develop_a_product_plan.summary: Roadmap gated on executing the MVBP, validating carrier acceptance, and growing real supply beyond ~4 in-conversation pilots; flags an unresolved engineering-resourcing gap

key_assumptions.statement: Assumes Part 107 drone pilots are willing to accept marketplace-dispatched jobs from multiple different roofing-contractor clients (rather than maintaining their own direct client relationships) and will accept surge-based job routing/prioritization rather than first-come-first-served.
key_assumptions.test_plan: Ask this directly in conversations with the 12 pilots in Derek's existing network (feeds Step 9's supply-side prospect list); if resistance is high, the marketplace may need a different dispatch model (pilot-choice bidding instead of platform-assigned routing).

key_assumptions.statement: Assumes Derek's 6 existing direct clients will adopt the marketplace booking flow rather than continuing to call Derek personally.
key_assumptions.test_plan: Route the next real storm-season booking from an existing client through the marketplace flow instead of a direct call and observe whether they accept it.

key_assumptions.statement: Supply-side profile is based on 8 conversations, all sourced from Derek's own pre-existing network — no supply-side conversations yet exist with a pilot Derek did not already know before starting this pivot, so the profile may be systematically biased toward 'people who already like Derek' rather than the broader addressable pilot population.
key_assumptions.test_plan: Recruit and interview at least 5 pilots with no prior relationship to Derek (e.g., via a cold post in a regional drone-operator group) before treating this profile as validated beyond his existing network.

key_assumptions.statement: Demand-side profile is based entirely on Derek's 6 existing direct clients — people who already trust him personally as a solo operator. Whether a roofing contractor with no prior relationship to Derek would trust a marketplace (vs. trusting Derek the person) is untested.
key_assumptions.test_plan: Interview at least 5 roofing contractors with no prior Osei Aerial relationship, sourced via the trade association, before treating demand-side trust dynamics as understood beyond Derek's existing book of business.

key_assumptions.statement: The 350-pilot commercially-active count is extrapolated from Facebook-group/meetup membership with an assumed 40% commercial-activity rate — not independently sourced.
key_assumptions.test_plan: Cross-check against FAA Part 107 certificate-holder data by ZIP/region if a usable public extract exists, or commission a targeted survey of the two Facebook groups.

key_assumptions.statement: This step's beachhead-TAM sanity-check heuristic (tens to low hundreds of millions/year) does not state whether it should be checked against GMV or against take-rate revenue for a marketplace business — applying it to the (correct, per this step's own formula) take-rate revenue figure makes an early-stage, supply-constrained marketplace look disqualified regardless of underlying market health.
key_assumptions.test_plan: Flag to the plugin maintainers as a methodology question, not something this business can resolve on its own — see QA-FINDINGS-ROUND3.md.

key_assumptions.statement: Marcus Webb is used as the primary persona partly because he's the most-interviewed, most-cooperative pilot in Derek's network — not confirmed as statistically representative of the broader 350-pilot supply-side population (many of whom Derek doesn't know personally).

key_assumptions.statement: Assumes a real-time pilot-availability display is what demand-side users actually need to trust the marketplace (vs., e.g., a guaranteed-response-time promise instead) — not yet tested with a real product.

key_assumptions.statement: Assumes a downloadable PDF/link report format is sufficient for contractors to submit to insurance carriers — not yet confirmed with a real carrier or adjuster.

key_assumptions.statement: Demand-side value is described directionally ('capacity unlock') but not reduced to a single dollar figure, because the actual volume of currently-missed business is unknown — treating this as a real gap rather than forcing a number that would be invented.

risk_log.description: Onboarding privacy/data-handling and legal-scope notice given to founder on 2026-08-18.

False precision (failure mode 2): plan/04-calculate-the-tam-for-the-beachhead-market.md's first draft stated the beachhead TAM as an exact '$882,000/year' and the demand-side ceiling as an exact '$23,100,000/year', despite every input to both figures being a founder estimate or extrapolation, several explicitly low-confidence. BLOCKING per the false-precision check. Resolution: rounded both to order-of-magnitude figures (≈$880,000/year and ≈$23M/year) and stated explicitly that the precise multiplication shown in the derivation is for arithmetic transparency, not a claim of dollar-level accuracy.
risk_log.status: mitigated — fix applied directly to plan/04-calculate-the-tam-for-the-beachhead-market.md and its quantitative_claims entries; gate re-run and returned PASS.

risk_log.description: Automation-bias advisory (failure mode 3, non-blocking): plan/14-calculate-the-tam-for-follow-on-markets.md's Pin 2 'additive TAM' framing could read as a clean incremental number to a skimming reader unless the supply-contention caveat (ka-014-pin2-supply-contention) is read in full. Recommended making the caveat more prominent if this file's figures are excerpted into the assembled plan.

Structural/methodology advisory (non-blocking, standing note): skills/disciplined-entrepreneurship/17-calculate-the-ltv-of-a-customer/SKILL.md and .../18-map-the-sales-process-to-acquire-a-customer/SKILL.md contain zero marketplace-specific branching, unlike every other DE step this business touched (01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 22, 23 all have marketplace guidance). This forced undocumented scope decisions while drafting plan/17-... and plan/18-...md (see ka-017-no-marketplace-guidance, ka-018-no-marketplace-guidance) and produced a real, demonstrated cross-step gap in plan/19-calculate-the-coca.md, where a supply-side COCA figure has no corresponding LTV to sanity-check it against. This does not make either file's own stated numbers unsourced or falsely precise (both are honestly scoped and flagged), so it is advisory against the plan, not blocking — but it is a real product/methodology gap in the plugin itself. See docs/QA-FINDINGS-ROUND3.md for the full writeup and recommended fix.

False precision (failure mode 2): plan/17-calculate-the-ltv-of-a-customer.md's first draft stated the LTV figure as an exact '$3,748.50', despite every input (ARPU, margin, churn/lifetime) being a low-confidence founder estimate or a single N-of-1 data point. BLOCKING per the false-precision check. Resolution: rounded to ≈$3,750 in the plan file and the qc-017-ltv entry.
risk_log.status: mitigated — fix applied directly to plan/17-calculate-the-ltv-of-a-customer.md and its quantitative_claims entry; gate re-run and returned PASS.

risk_log.description: Unsourced claim (failure mode 1): plan/23-show-that-dogs-will-eat-the-dog-food.md's 'Prior-operating-history data point' section stated Osei Aerial's historical client rebooking rate ('roughly 78%') as fact with no matching quantitative_claims entry — the same failure mode round 2's QA findings documented for a different business's Step 17 (a step drafts a real figure into prose and forgets the matching entry). Surfaced when plan/business-plan.md (which repeats this figure in the Executive Summary and Confidence & Validation Status section) went through assemble-business-plan's own mandatory pre-assembly AI-risk gate (§7.5). BLOCKING per the Data Contract's unsourced-number rule. Resolution: added qc-023-legacy-rebooking-rate to business-state.json and to plan/23-show-that-dogs-will-eat-the-dog-food.md.
risk_log.status: mitigated — entry added to both business-state.json and the originating step file; gate re-run on plan/business-plan.md and returned PASS.
